title: David and Jonathan
hook: David mourns Jonathan's love as wonderful

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ruth on the road. Your line was where you go. Did you take a step toward the person you chose to stay with? Today, another kind of loyalty: two friends. Day eight hundred twenty-eight.

"Thy love to me was wonderful, passing the love of women." A warrior sings that over a dead friend. The news has just reached David: King Saul and his son Jonathan have fallen in battle on Mount Gilboa. Saul has hunted David. Jonathan was Saul's son, the heir to the throne David would one day take. By the usual rules of politics, they should have been rivals. Instead, near the end of David's lament come Jonathan's name and that line. Today: how that friendship began, what it cost, and what David did with it after the funeral.
screen: `THY LOVE TO ME WAS WONDERFUL.` → `THE KING'S SON, AND HIS RIVAL.` → `BEGINNING, COST, AND AFTER.`

segments.voice: It begins with a sentence that doesn't sound like politics at all. After David's victory over Goliath, the text says "the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul." Knit, like two threads. Then Jonathan does something startling. He takes off his own robe and gives it to David, with his sword, his bow and his belt. Some readers see a prince handing over the signs of his rank. Then the friendship gets expensive. Saul turns on David and wants him dead, and Jonathan is caught between his father and his friend. He warns David, at real risk to himself. Later, the text has him say it outright: you shall be king over Israel, and I shall be next to you. The heir steps aside in his own words. Readers have heard this bond in more than one way, and the text itself calls it love and a covenant. Then comes what David did after the grief. After the lament, after David becomes king, he asks a question nobody needed him to ask: "Is there yet any that is left of the house of Saul, that I may shew him kindness for Jonathan's sake?" There is: Jonathan's son Mephibosheth, lame in both feet, living quietly far from court. David sends for him, gives him back his grandfather's land, and seats him at the king's table for good. Kindness here is that same Hebrew word from yesterday, chesed. The friend is gone. The friendship keeps going, now as a seat at the table for his son.
screen: `TWO SOULS KNIT TOGETHER.` · `A PRINCE GIVES AWAY HIS ROBE.` · `CAUGHT BETWEEN FATHER AND FRIEND.` · `A SEAT AT THE TABLE FOR HIS SON.` · then, large: `FOR JONATHAN'S SAKE.`

segments.voice: Let an old friend come to mind. Someone who once stood next to you, at school, at work, in a hard year, and whom life has carried somewhere else. Breathe, and remember one specific thing: a joke, a kitchen, a drive, something they did for you. Hold it for a few breaths. Then let a first sentence of a note form in your head. Not an apology for the silence. Just the memory, and that you thought of them. If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name. The bell holds the time.
David and Jonathan. A king's son and the man who would take his father's throne, knit together as friends, with a kindness that outlived Jonathan. Today's word.
Your line: the friend. Today, write to that old friend, even three lines, and send it. Day eight hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Readers of the Hebrew Bible point to David and Jonathan as a picture of loyal friendship, and some keep up old friendships with letters, calls or visits on anniversaries and holidays.

fork.reveal: David asks whether anyone is left of Saul's house, finds Jonathan's son Mephibosheth, returns his land and seats him at his table.

original.note: Hebrew: covenant, a binding promise. Jonathan and David make one because Jonathan loved him as his own soul.

trapdoor: what you thought: two war buddies.
what it means: the king's heir and the man who would take the throne, bound by love and a covenant.
what a scholar hears: chesed again, the same word as in Ruth: David's kindness to Mephibosheth is loyalty kept after the friend is gone.
